q: What are the length and width of the playing surface of the table?
detail: The playing surface is rectangular, **2.74 m long** and **1.525 m wide**, lying in a horizontal plane.

q: How high above the floor is the playing surface?
detail: The playing surface lies in a horizontal plane **76 cm** above the floor.

q: A standard ball dropped onto the playing surface from 30 cm should bounce to about what height?
options: About 23 cm
About 15 cm
About 26 cm
About 30 cm
detail: The surface may be of any material but must give a uniform bounce of **about 23 cm** when a standard ball is dropped from **30 cm**.

q: Are the vertical sides of the tabletop part of the playing surface?
options: No, the vertical sides are not part of the playing surface
Yes, the whole tabletop counts
Only the top 2 cm of the sides
Only in doubles
detail: The playing surface **does not include the vertical sides** of the tabletop. A ball that touches the side is not a good return, which is why edge and side decisions matter.

q: What colour and finish must the playing surface be, and what lines are marked on it?
a: Uniformly dark and matt, with white lines
detail: A **white side line 2 cm wide** runs along each 2.74 m edge and a **white end line 2 cm wide** along each 1.525 m edge. For doubles there is also a 3 mm white centre line.

q: How wide are the white side lines and end lines?
detail: Side lines and end lines are **2 cm** wide. The doubles centre line is much narrower: **3 mm**.

q: In doubles, the 3 mm centre line belongs to which half-court?
options: Each right half-court
Each left half-court
Neither: a ball on it is a fault
The server's choice
detail: The centre line is **regarded as part of each right half-court**, so a doubles service landing on the centre line is good.

q: How high is the top of the net above the playing surface, along its whole length?
detail: The top of the net, along its whole length, is **15.25 cm** above the playing surface.
hint: 15.25 cm is also the height of the net posts and their distance outside the side line.

q: How high are the net posts, and where are they placed?
a: 15.25 cm high, 15.25 cm outside the side line
detail: The net is suspended by a cord attached at each end to an upright post **15.25 cm high**, with the outside limits of the post **15.25 cm outside the side line**.

q: What does the “net assembly” consist of?
a: Net, suspension, supporting posts and clamps
detail: The net assembly is the **net, its suspension and the supporting posts, including the clamps** attaching them to the table. This matters because a player touching any part of it loses the point, and a service touching any part of it can be a let.

q: What is the diameter of the ball?
detail: The ball is spherical with a diameter of **40 mm**.

q: How much does the ball weigh?
detail: The ball weighs **2.7 g**.

q: Which ball meets the laws?
options: Plastic, white or orange, matt
Celluloid, any bright colour, glossy
Plastic, yellow or orange, glossy
Any material, white only, matt
detail: The ball must be made of **plastic** material and be **white or orange, and matt**.

q: At least what percentage of the racket blade, by thickness, must be natural wood?
detail: At least **85%** of the blade by thickness must be natural wood. An adhesive layer within the blade may be reinforced with fibrous material such as carbon fibre, up to 7.5% of the total thickness or 0.35 mm, whichever is smaller.

q: What is the maximum total thickness of sandwich rubber, including adhesive?
options: 4.0 mm
2.0 mm
3.5 mm
4.5 mm
detail: Sandwich rubber (pimples in or out) may be at most **4.0 mm** including adhesive. Ordinary pimpled rubber may be at most **2.0 mm** including adhesive.

q: What colours must the two sides of the racket be?
a: Black on one side, a bright colour on the other
detail: Each side must be **matt**: **black on one side**, and on the other a **bright colour clearly distinguishable from black and from the colour of the ball**. This applies whether the side is covered or left uncovered.

q: What do the laws say about the size, shape and weight of the racket?
options: Any size, shape or weight, but the blade must be flat and rigid
Maximum 30 cm long and 200 g
It must be round or oval
Weight is free but the blade must be at most 7 mm thick
detail: The racket **may be of any size, shape or weight**, but the **blade shall be flat and rigid**.

q: When must a player show their racket to the opponent and the umpire?
a: Before the match, and whenever they change racket during it
detail: Before the start of a match and **whenever a player changes racket** during a match, they must show the racket to the opponent and the umpire and allow them to examine it.

q: What is a “rally”?
a: The period during which the ball is in play
detail: A rally is **the period during which the ball is in play**. It ends when it is decided as a let or a point.

q: When does the ball come into play, and when does it stop being in play?
a: From the last moment it is stationary on the server's free palm, until the rally is decided
detail: The ball is in play **from the last moment at which it is stationary on the palm of the free hand before being intentionally projected in service**, until the rally is decided as a **let or a point**. So if the ball accidentally rolls off the hand before the toss, no point is scored.

q: What is the difference between a let and a point?
options: A let is a rally whose result is not scored; a point is a rally whose result is scored
A let is a service fault; a point is any other rally
A let is replayed only in service; a point is any rally
There is no difference in singles
detail: A **let** is a rally of which the result is **not scored**. A **point** is a rally of which the result **is scored**.

q: Define the “racket hand” and the “free hand”.
a: Racket hand carries the racket; free hand does not
detail: The **racket hand** is the hand carrying the racket. The **free hand** is the hand not carrying the racket, and the free arm is the arm of the free hand. A player may switch the racket between hands during play; whichever hand holds it becomes the racket hand.

q: During a rally the ball hits the fingers of the player's racket hand (below the wrist) and goes over onto the opponent's court. Is it a good return?
options: Yes: touching it with the racket hand below the wrist counts as striking
No: only the racket may strike the ball
Only if the racket also touched it
It is a let
detail: A player **strikes** the ball if they touch it in play **with the racket held in the hand, or with the racket hand below the wrist**. Throwing the racket at the ball, or hitting it with the hand after dropping the racket, is not striking.

q: Who is the “server” and who is the “receiver”?
a: Server strikes first in a rally; receiver strikes second
detail: The **server** is the player due to strike the ball **first** in a rally. The **receiver** is the player due to strike it **second**.

q: For the purposes of the laws, how far does the end line extend?
options: Indefinitely in both directions
Only across the width of the table
To the net posts
To the surrounds
detail: The end line is **regarded as extending indefinitely in both directions**. This matters for the service rule that the ball must be behind the server's end line.

q: How do the laws define the umpire and the assistant umpire?
a: Umpire controls the match; AU assists with certain decisions
detail: The **umpire** is the person appointed **to control a match**. The **assistant umpire** is the person appointed **to assist the umpire with certain decisions**.

q: How must the service start?
a: Ball resting freely on the open palm of the stationary free hand
detail: Service starts with the ball **resting freely on the open palm** of the server's **stationary free hand**. The open palm is there so the ball cannot be gripped or spun.

q: In service, at least how high must the ball rise after leaving the palm of the free hand?
detail: The ball must rise **at least 16 cm** after leaving the palm, then fall without touching anything before being struck.
hint: 16 cm is just above the net height (15.25 cm), so the net is a handy reference.

q: How must the server project the ball?
options: Near vertically upwards, without imparting spin
Upwards at any angle up to 45°, without spin
Near vertically upwards; spin is allowed
In any direction, as long as it rises 16 cm
detail: The ball must be projected **near vertically upwards, without imparting spin**. “Near vertically” means within a few degrees of vertical. The old 45° limit no longer applies.

q: Where must a served ball bounce in singles, and in doubles?
a: Server's court, then receiver's court. In doubles: right half-court to right half-court
detail: As the ball falls, the server strikes it so it touches **first their own court and then directly the receiver's court**. In doubles it must touch successively the **right half-court of server and receiver**.

q: From the start of service until it is struck, where must the ball be?
options: Above the level of the playing surface and behind the server's end line
Above the net height and behind the end line
Anywhere, as long as it is visible to the receiver
Behind the end line; height does not matter
detail: From the start of service until struck, the ball must be **above the level of the playing surface** and **behind the server's end line**.

q: During service, who must be able to see the ball, and what must not hide it?
a: The receiver; it must not be hidden by the server, their partner or anything they wear or carry
detail: The ball **shall not be hidden from the receiver** by the server or their doubles partner, or by anything they wear or carry. As soon as the ball is projected, the **free arm and hand must be removed** from the space between the ball and the net.

q: What makes a return good?
options: It touches the opponent's court directly or after touching the net assembly
It touches the opponent's court directly; touching the net is a fault
It passes over the net and lands anywhere on the table
It touches the opponent's court within two bounces
detail: The ball, having been served or returned, must be struck so that it touches the **opponent's court, either directly or after touching the net assembly**. A net touch in a rally (not in service) is not a let.

q: What is the order of play in singles?
a: Server serves, receiver returns, then they alternate
detail: In singles the **server makes a service**, the **receiver makes a return**, and thereafter server and receiver **alternately** each make a return.

q: In doubles (no wheelchair players), what is the order of play?
options: Server, receiver, server's partner, receiver's partner, then repeat
Server, server's partner, receiver, receiver's partner
Server, receiver, then either player of each pair
Server, receiver's partner, server's partner, receiver
detail: The **server** serves, the **receiver** returns, then the **partner of the server**, then the **partner of the receiver**, and each player in turn continues in that sequence. Striking out of sequence loses the point (“wrong player”).

q: An otherwise correct service touches the net, then bounces on the receiver's court. What is your decision?
options: Let
Point to the server
Point to the receiver
Play on: a net touch is fine

diagram.alt: Side view: the service clips the top of the net, then bounces on the receiver's court

detail: If in service the ball touches the net assembly, the rally is a **let**, provided the service is otherwise correct (or the ball is obstructed by the receiver or partner). If it then misses the receiver's court, the receiver scores a point.

umpire.signal: Raise one arm above the head once the ball has touched the correct court

q: During a rally, a player's shirt brushes the net while the ball is in play. What is your decision?
options: Point to the opponent
Let
No decision: clothing doesn't count
Point to that player if their shot was good
detail: A player scores a point if their opponent, **or anything the opponent wears or carries, touches the net assembly**. Explanation term: “touched net”.

umpire.signal: Raise the arm nearer the winner, upper arm horizontal, forearm vertical, closed hand
umpire.call: New score, and “touched net” if an explanation is needed

q: While stretching for a wide ball, a player puts their free hand on the playing surface to keep balance. The ball is still in play. What is your decision?
options: Point to the opponent
Let
Play on: it was only for balance
Point to the opponent only if the table moved
detail: A player scores a point if their **opponent's free hand touches the playing surface**. This applies whether or not the player would have made a good return. Explanation term: “hand on table”.

umpire.call: New score, and “hand on table” if needed

q: What happens if a player moves the playing surface while the ball is in play?
a: The opponent scores a point
detail: A point is scored if an opponent, or anything they wear or carry, **moves the playing surface**. In practice umpires only penalise lifting, permanent shifting, displacement or intentional shaking. A light knock that barely moves a hinged table is not usually penalised. Explanation term: “moved table”.

q: After being struck by the opponent, the ball flies past the end line of a player's court without touching it. Who scores?
options: The player whose court it passed over
The opponent who struck it
Nobody: it is a let
Whoever touched it last
detail: A player scores if the ball **passes over their court or beyond their end line without touching their court**, after being struck by the opponent.

q: How is a game won?
a: First to 11 points, or a 2-point lead after 10-10
detail: A game is won by the player or pair **first scoring 11 points**, unless both reach **10 points**, when it is won by the first to gain a **lead of 2 points**.

q: The score is 10-10. Which of these scores ends the game?
detail: After 10-10 the game goes on until one side leads by **2 points**, so 12-10, 13-11, 14-12 and so on.

q: How many games can a match consist of?
options: The best of any odd number of games
Always the best of 5 games
Always the best of 7 games
Any number of games agreed by the players
detail: A match consists of **the best of any odd number of games**, commonly best of 3, 5 or 7. The competition sets which.

q: How is the right to choose serving, receiving or ends decided, and what can the winner choose?
a: By lot. The winner chooses to serve, to receive, or which end to start
detail: The right to choose is **decided by lot**, usually a coin or two-coloured disc toss. The winner may choose to **serve first, receive first, or start at a particular end**.

q: The toss winner chooses to serve first. What does the opponent get to choose?
options: Which end to start at
Nothing more
Whether to serve or receive in game 2
The match ball
detail: When one side has chosen to serve, receive or an end, **the other side has the other choice**. Both players make a choice.

q: In normal play, after how many points does service change?
detail: After **every 2 points** the receiving player or pair becomes the serving player or pair.

q: What changes in the serving rotation once the score reaches 10-10?
options: Each player serves for only 1 point in turn
Service changes every 2 points as before
The player who served first serves until the game ends
The players change ends
detail: When both sides reach **10 points** (or the expedite system is in operation), the serving sequence stays the same but **each player serves for only 1 point** in turn.

q: What changes between one game and the next?
a: Ends switch, and whoever served first now receives first
detail: The player or pair **serving first in a game receives first in the next game**, and the player or pair starting at one end **starts at the other end** in the next game.

q: What is the umpire's primary duty?
a: To decide the result of each rally
detail: For each match there is an umpire whose **primary duty is to decide the result of each rally**. In principle the umpire has no discretionary powers but must use judgment in applying some laws, such as lets for outside disturbances or acceptable behaviour.

q: Who is the sole authority on questions of rule interpretation during a competition?
options: The referee (or an authorised deputy)
The umpire
The assistant umpire
The tournament organiser
detail: The **referee**, or an authorised deputy, must be in the playing hall throughout play to decide any question of **rule interpretation**, on which they are the **sole authority**.

q: Where should the umpire be positioned?
options: About 2–3 m from the side of the table, in line with the net
Behind one end of the table
About 1 m from the net post, standing
Anywhere with a clear view
detail: The umpire sits about **2–3 metres from the side of the table, in line with the net**, preferably on a slightly raised chair. Standing is not recommended for singles because it blocks spectators.

q: Where does the assistant umpire sit?
a: Directly opposite the umpire, in line with the net
detail: The assistant umpire sits **directly opposite the umpire, in line with the net**, at about the same distance from the table. The AU should not stand for doubles.

q: For up to how many minutes may players practise at the table before the match?
detail: Players may practise for **up to 2 minutes**. If they finish sooner, they should start play at once.

q: How long may the interval between games last, at most?
detail: Each interval between games is limited to **1 minute**. Time not used at one interval cannot be claimed at the next.

q: How many time-outs is each player or pair entitled to in an individual match, and how long is each?
options: One, of up to 1 minute
One per game, of up to 1 minute
Two, of up to 1 minute each
One, of up to 2 minutes
detail: Each player or pair (or their captain or adviser) may take **one time-out of up to 1 minute** during an individual match, requested with a **T-sign** between rallies.

q: What is the basic rule on the colour of playing clothing?
a: The main colour must be clearly different from the ball
detail: The **main colour** of clothing must be **clearly different from the colour of the ball** in use, so the ball stays visible. “Main” does not necessarily mean the largest area. The back of the shirt can be disregarded for this purpose.

q: Must opposing players wear shirts of different colours?
options: Yes, except in WTT events
Only in team matches
No, only the ball colour matters
Only if a spectator complains
detail: **Except in WTT events**, opposing players and pairs must wear shirts of **different colours**. The umpire should settle this before practice, preferably in the Call Area.

q: Opposing shirts are too similar and neither player will agree to change. It has been decided one must change. How is it decided who?
options: The umpire decides by lot
The higher-ranked player keeps their shirt
The player who arrived second changes
The referee picks
detail: The umpire first asks the players to decide. If one must change and they cannot agree who, **the umpire decides by lot**. If they do not accept the umpire's ruling that their shirts are too similar, the referee is called.

q: When calling the score, whose score does the umpire call first?
options: The player or pair due to serve next
The player or pair who won the last point
The player or pair on the umpire's right
The player or pair who is leading
detail: The umpire calls **first the score of the player or pair due to serve next**, then the opponents' score. At a change of service, the umpire points to the next server.

q: What does the umpire announce at the start of a game?
a: “[Name] to serve, love-all” (or “zero-zero”)
detail: Point to the server and announce, e.g. **“Keen to serve, love-all”** or “zero-zero”, so players don't start before the call is complete. 0 may be called “zero” or “love”.

q: The umpire declares a let. What score does the umpire call?
options: Repeat the existing score
Call nothing
Call the score with a point added to the server
Call “let” only, no score
detail: If the rally is a let, the umpire **repeats the existing score** to confirm that no point has been scored.

q: Which hand signal does the umpire use to declare a let?
options: Raise one hand above the head
Point with an open hand to the server
Raise the arm nearer the receiver, forearm vertical
Cross both arms
detail: For a let, or to delay the resumption of play, the umpire **raises one hand above the head**. The AU uses the same signal to attract the umpire's attention.
